old:
идти́ — to go, walk. е́хать — to go by vehicle, ride. The first describes movement on foot; the second movement by vehicle. These are different means of moving, not an aspect pair.

Classify идти́ as unidirectional: motion in one direction. Its other column is multidirectional, covering repeated, return or different-direction movement according to context. These directionality labels are not English verb meanings. The basic unprefixed forms in these columns are imperfective; unidirectional does not itself mean perfective or arrival.

нести́ — to carry. вести́ — to lead; it can also mean to drive a vehicle. везти́ — to convey, transport. Carrying on foot, leading someone and transporting by vehicle are distinct meanings.

Он пошёл к другу. — he set off toward a friend. The perfective prefixed verb presents the beginning of the journey; it does not say that he arrived. Он шёл к другу. — He was on his way to a friend's place. This English rendering accompanies an imperfective form describing motion toward the friend; the Russian form alone does not specify how long he was on the way. The reading he was already on the way for a long time adds a long duration that the sentence does not state, and he refused to go contradicts the setting-out sentence.

Мальчик отошёл от незнакомца — The boy stepped back from the stranger. The verb and the phrase after it express movement away from the stranger. There is no additional relative clause in this displayed sentence. Они улетят из Владивостока через месяц. — They will leave Vladivostok in a month. Мяч залетел на крышу дома. — The ball flew onto the roof of the house. These are different subjects and paths. The prefix contributes to the motion meaning, while the accompanying phrases identify the path and time; do not substitute a translation of a different example.

Мы идём в библиотеку. — We are headed to the library. Птицы летят на юг. — The birds are flying south. These supplied contexts show Motion in progress in one direction (imperfective). Ребёнок ходит шесть месяцев. — The child has been walking for six months. This is General walking ability (imperfective). Мы ходили по городу весь день. — We walked around the city all day. This is Movement in various directions (imperfective). Directionality is a property of the whole supplied use, not an English lexical gloss or an automatic claim that the traveller arrived. The basic unprefixed pairs are imperfective.

Она ходит в супермаркет каждую неделю. — She goes to the supermarket every week. This is Repeated trips (imperfective). В прошлом году я ездил в Россию. — I went to Russia (and returned) last year. In the context this is One completed round trip in the past (imperfective). In this example the past round-trip interpretation includes a return; the unprefixed form nevertheless remains imperfective. The statement “The form is perfective because this trip is completed.” is wrong: a completed trip does not make these verb forms perfective. Do not equate a destination with unidirectionality or event completion with perfective aspect. Prefixed setting-out and path examples require their separately taught meanings.

Each unidirectional verb has a multidirectional partner: идти́ and ходи́ть, е́хать and е́здить, нести́ and носи́ть, вести́ and води́ть, везти́ and вози́ть. Practise writing each verb from its meaning and from its partner. Past forms agree with the subject: шёл is the masculine past form of идти́, пошёл of пойти́, and отошёл of отойти́. ездил is the masculine past form of е́здить. Present forms agree with the subject's person and number: идём is the we form of идти́, and ходит is the he or she form of ходи́ть. For flying, летят is the unidirectional they form and летают the multidirectional they form. Мы идём в библиотеку. Птицы летят на юг. Ребёнок ходит шесть месяцев. В прошлом году я ездил в Россию. Practise writing each of these forms from the verb it belongs to.

old:
два — дво́е. три — тро́е. A cardinal states a quantity; a collective presents that quantity as a group. An ordinal states position in a sequence. Thus дво́е is the collective for two, and тро́е is the collective for three. The option второ́й means second, and тре́тий means third; these are ordinal positions, not collective quantities.

Collective number forms are not a general replacement for cardinal numbers with every noun. Standard uses include groups of male people, children or people expressed by appropriate group nouns, personal pronouns, and certain nouns used only in the plural. Use ordinary cardinals with female-person nouns in standard usage; do not infer that any feminine noun takes a collective. This lesson explains the restriction without introducing new Russian noun combinations.
